newsitem.title: BURMA: Burma's SLORC brushes off U.S. economic sanctions.
newsitem.headline: Burma's SLORC brushes off U.S. economic sanctions.

text.p: One of Burma's military leaders on Tuesday played down the impact of U.S. economic sanctions against his country and denied Western allegations of human rights abuses.
"It's not a problem for us," Lieutenant-General Khin Nyunt told foreign journalists accompanying a government trip to the Golden Triangle area in eastern Shan state.
Khin Nyunt, the powerful military intelligence chief and Secretary One of the State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC), said the U.S. move was no surprise.
"In politics you have to expect such things," he said.
"We don't feel very sorry about this because we have many friends in countries around the region who understand us," Khin Nyunt said. "So we can work it out."
"We have five neighbours...we have very good border trade," he said.

The U.S. State Department was due to officially announce economic sanctions on Burma later on Tuesday, an administration official said in Washington. The sanctions, which have already been approved by President Bill Clinton, will ban new U.S. investment in Burma.
The U.S. is the fourth-largest investor in Burma in terms of approved foreign investment.
Asked whether Burma's military rulers would reconsider government policy because of the sanctions move, he said: "We don't have anything to reconsider because we are walking in a straight line.
"We have decided we will not stray (from our course)."
Khin Nyunt said U.S. and Western charges against the SLORC of human rights violations were unfounded.
"Politics is played by some people in Rangoon, but in the country areas everything is running normally," he said.

The SLORC has been accused by human rights organisations and many Western governments of abuses, such as summary executions, using forced labour and employing repressive tactics against the opposition.
The SLORC has also been condemned for failing to recognise the 1990 landslide electoral victory of the National League for Democracy (NLD) party co-founded by Nobel Peace laureate Aung San Suu Kyi.
Suu Kyi was kept under house arrest for six years until mid-1995 for her criticism of the Rangoon government.
Several American companies have pulled out of the country over the past few years because of pressure by human rights organisations.
Major companies still doing business there include oil companies Unocal Corp and Atlantic Richfield Co.
Unocal, the largest U.S. investor in Burma, said on Tuesday it was disappointed by the sanctions move but that this would not affect its investment policy in the region.
